decks.domain: Rules of the road: lights, speed, following, required stops and right-of-way

cards.front: Must you obey a traffic officer who tells you to do something normally illegal?
cards.back: You must obey a traffic officer at all times, even when told to do something normally illegal, such as driving through a red light behind a funeral procession.

cards.front: Why should you never coast downhill in neutral or with the clutch pressed?
cards.back: Never coast downhill in neutral, and in a manual car never coast with the clutch pressed, because both reduce your control.

cards.front: Which way do you go around traffic circles in Tennessee?
cards.back: Tennessee drives on the right, so you go to the right around traffic circles, roundabouts and town squares.

cards.front: During which hours must headlights be on?
cards.back: Headlights must be on from thirty minutes after sunset until thirty minutes before sunrise.
cards.memory_hook: Thirty after sunset, thirty before sunrise

cards.front: When else are headlights required?
cards.back: Headlights are also required whenever you cannot clearly see people or vehicles two hundred feet ahead, and whenever rain, mist or snow keeps your wipers running.

cards.front: When must you dim your high beams?
cards.back: Dim your high beams when an oncoming vehicle comes within five hundred feet or when you are within five hundred feet behind another vehicle.

cards.front: Which lights may you not drive with alone when visibility is limited?
cards.back: Driving with only parking lights on when visibility is limited is illegal, and so is using fog or auxiliary lights alone or when high beams must be dimmed.

cards.front: What lights must a stopped or parked vehicle show when visibility is limited?
cards.back: A vehicle stopped or parked on the road or shoulder must show parking lights when visibility is limited, even though driving on parking lights alone is illegal then.

cards.front: What colors may steady front-facing lights be?
cards.back: Since January one, two thousand eighteen, steady lights showing to the front of a vehicle must be white or amber, with exceptions for certain vehicles.

cards.front: Which flashing front-facing lights are allowed?
cards.back: Also since January one, two thousand eighteen, no flashing front-facing lights are allowed other than factory emergency flashers, again with some vehicle exceptions.

cards.front: How must loose loads be carried?
cards.back: Any vehicle carrying litter or loose material that could fall or blow onto the highway must keep it enclosed or fully covered by a tarp.

cards.front: What penalties apply to littering?
cards.back: Littering fines run from fifty dollars to three thousand dollars by amount, plus up to forty hours of litter pickup and, if the court chooses, up to eight hours at a recycling center.

cards.front: What are the rules for a funeral procession on a two-lane road?
cards.back: On a two-lane road you may not pass a funeral procession, and you may not drive between its vehicles unless an officer directs you to.

decks.domain: Rules of the road: lights, speed, following, required stops and right-of-way

cards.front: When is driving slowly illegal?
cards.back: Driving below a posted minimum speed in normal conditions is illegal, and even with no minimum posted you may not drive so slowly that you block traffic.

cards.front: When do you count as a slow-moving vehicle, and when must you pull off?
cards.back: You count as a slow-moving vehicle at ten miles per hour or more below the speed limit, and with five or more vehicles lined up behind you, you must pull off when safe.

cards.front: When is driving below a posted minimum allowed?
cards.back: Driving below a posted minimum is allowed in bad weather, heavy traffic or on a bad road.

cards.front: What is the Basic Speed Rule?
cards.back: The Basic Speed Rule is a safety principle rather than a Tennessee law: your speed must fit current conditions, and driving faster than conditions allow breaks the rule even below the posted limit.

cards.front: How far ahead must you always be able to stop under the Basic Speed Rule?
cards.back: Under the Basic Speed Rule your speed must always let you stop within the clear distance you can see ahead.

cards.front: What does the Basic Speed Rule take into account?
cards.back: The Basic Speed Rule weighs traffic volume and speed, pedestrians, road surface, width and layout, visibility, weather and your own ability.

cards.front: If you rear-end a car that stopped suddenly, what does that show?
cards.back: If the car ahead stops suddenly and you cannot avoid hitting it, you were breaking the Basic Speed Rule or following too closely, even within the limit.

cards.front: Are slow drivers safer than speeders?
cards.back: The manual says slow drivers are as likely to crash as speeders, so keep pace with traffic that is moving within the limit.

cards.front: What is the speed limit on state and federal highways unless posted otherwise?
cards.back: Unless another limit is posted, primary and secondary state and federal highways have a fifty-five miles per hour speed limit.

cards.front: What are Tennessee's top rural and typical urban interstate limits?
cards.back: Tennessee's top interstate speed limit is seventy miles per hour, posted on most rural interstate sections, while congested urban interstates are typically fifty-five miles per hour

cards.front: What are the minimum speeds in the left and right interstate lanes?
cards.back: Driving under fifty-five miles per hour in the far left lane of an interstate is illegal unless congestion prevents it, and the minimum in the right lanes is forty-five miles per hour

cards.front: What should you do if the interstate minimum is too fast for you?
cards.back: If the interstate minimum speed is too fast for you, take another road.

cards.front: Who sets speed limits on Tennessee roads?
cards.back: The state, counties and cities each set speed limits on their own roads, and some residential streets are limited to twenty-five or thirty-five miles per hour at all times.

decks.domain: Rules of the road: lights, speed, following, required stops and right-of-way

cards.front: How does the law treat speeding in a school zone?
cards.back: Speeding in a school zone is treated by law as reckless driving and adds an automatic six points to your record, which triggers an advisory letter.

cards.front: When do school zone speed limits apply?
cards.back: School zone limits apply while children are going to or from school and during recess.

cards.front: What fine does Tennessee law set for speeding in an active work zone?
cards.back: Tennessee law sets a fine of at least two hundred fifty dollars and up to five hundred dollars for speeding in an active work zone.

cards.front: What counts as a work zone, and how is it marked?
cards.back: Work zones include utility work, tree trimming and surveying, and are marked by orange or yellow-green signs, flashing equipment lights and brightly dressed workers.

cards.front: What do the manual's work zone crash figures show?
cards.back: The manual reports that Tennessee work zone crashes in two thousand twenty-one killed twenty-six people, injured one thousand one hundred five and caused three thousand ten property damage cases.

decks.domain: Rules of the road: lights, speed, following, required stops and right-of-way

cards.front: How should you brake in normal driving?
cards.back: Brake early, slowly and evenly; braking too hard can make you skid, and sudden stops make it harder for drivers behind you to stop.

cards.front: In a car without anti-lock brakes, what should you do if you start to skid?
cards.back: In a car without anti-lock brakes, if you start to skid, take your foot off the brake and steer in the direction of the skid when it is safe to do so.

cards.front: How should you brake hard with anti-lock brakes?
cards.back: With anti-lock brakes, press firmly and steadily, never pump the pedal, and steer around hazards while keeping your foot on the brake until you stop.

cards.front: What should you expect from the pedal when anti-lock brakes work?
cards.back: Noise and vibration in the pedal are normal when anti-lock brakes work, and lifting off or pumping the pedal disengages them.

cards.front: How do covering the brake and riding the brake differ?
cards.back: Covering the brake, holding your foot just above it for a quick response, is a safe habit, but riding the brake, resting your foot on it, is not.

cards.front: Why is riding the brake harmful?
cards.back: Riding the brake wears out the brakes and falsely tells drivers behind that you are about to stop.

cards.front: How many ways of applying the brakes must every car have?
cards.back: By law every car needs two separate ways of applying the brakes, usually the foot brake and a parking or emergency brake.

cards.front: How can you slow a manual car for a stop?
cards.back: In a manual car you can slow for a stop by first flashing your brake lights to warn drivers behind, then shifting to a lower gear.

cards.front: What causes most rear-end crashes?
cards.back: Most rear-end crashes are caused by tailgating, which also blocks your view of the road ahead.

cards.front: What does Tennessee law say about following too closely?
cards.back: Tennessee law forbids following another vehicle more closely than is reasonable for the speed, traffic and road conditions.

cards.front: How does the two-second rule work?
cards.back: Under the two-second rule, start counting as the car ahead passes a fixed point; if you reach that point before two seconds, you are following too closely.

cards.front: What should you do if the two-second count shows you are too close?
cards.back: If the two-second count shows you are too close, ease off and recheck at another fixed point until you are at least two seconds back.

cards.front: When should you increase following distance to at least four seconds?
cards.back: Increase your following distance to at least four seconds in bad weather, at night, at interstate speeds and when following a motorcycle.

cards.front: What are the three steps of stopping?
cards.back: Stopping takes three steps: perception time to recognize danger, reaction time to start braking, which averages about two-thirds of a second, and braking time.

cards.front: In the manual's deer example at seventy miles per hour, how far does a driver travel?
cards.back: The manual's example shows that at seventy miles per hour a driver who spots a deer travels one hundred twenty-eight feet before braking and needs about four hundred eighteen feet in all to stop.

cards.front: What affects stopping distance?
cards.back: Stopping distance depends on the pavement, tires, brakes, shock absorbers and the vehicle's weight when loaded or towing.

cards.front: How far does a light passenger car need to stop at fifty miles per hour, per the National Safety Council?
cards.back: The manual cites the National Safety Council: a light passenger car at fifty miles per hour can stop in about two hundred feet.

decks.domain: Rules of the road: lights, speed, following, required stops and right-of-way

cards.front: Where must you stop at a stop sign?
cards.back: At a stop sign you must stop at a marked stop line or before the nearest side of the crosswalk; with neither, stop where you can see cross traffic but before entering the intersection.

cards.front: How does Tennessee law define a stop?
cards.back: Tennessee law defines a stop as the complete end of all movement, and a right turn on red also requires a full stop first.

cards.front: How much room should you leave when stopped behind another vehicle?
cards.back: When stopped behind another vehicle, leave enough room to see its rear tires touching the pavement, giving you space to steer around it if needed.

cards.front: What can a rolling stop cost you?
cards.back: A rolling stop is illegal and is grounds both for a ticket and for failing the road test.

cards.front: What should you do if you cannot see cross traffic after stopping?
cards.back: If you cannot see cross traffic after stopping, edge forward slowly until you can see both ways, and wait for anyone in the crosswalk to finish crossing.

cards.front: After the car ahead clears the intersection, what must you do?
cards.back: After the car ahead clears the intersection, pull up to the stop line and come to a full stop again yourself.

cards.front: How can you tell your car has fully stopped?
cards.back: Officers and instructors say a car has fully stopped only when you feel it lurch forward after all motion ends.

cards.front: Whose stop signals at construction sites must you obey?
cards.back: You must stop completely when a flagger at a construction site or a police officer signals you to stop.

cards.front: How should you approach a railroad crossing?
cards.back: Drive at a speed that lets you stop before the nearest rail, and do not cross until every track is clear of trains.

cards.front: Where should you stop when a train is approaching?
cards.back: When a train is approaching, stop between fifteen and fifty feet from the tracks, never on them, and wait until it has passed and crossing is safe.

cards.front: When must trains sound their horn, and what signs mean do not cross?
cards.back: Trains must sound their horn about one thousand five hundred feet before a crossing, and flashing lights, a lowered gate, a flagger or a visible train all mean you must not cross.

cards.front: What pavement markings warn of a railroad crossing?
cards.back: Railroad crossing pavement markings include a large X, the letters RR, a no-passing stripe and a stop line, and breaking railroad signals carries the same penalties as other traffic devices.

cards.front: Which vehicles must stop at every railroad crossing?
cards.back: School and church buses, taxis and other passenger carriers for hire, and vehicles carrying flammable, explosive or hazardous cargo must stop at every railroad crossing.

cards.front: How do buses and tankers signal a stop at a railroad crossing?
cards.back: A bus about to stop at a railroad crossing pulls right with its stoplights on, and tankers required to stop usually turn on emergency flashers.

decks.domain: Rules of the road: lights, speed, following, required stops and right-of-way

cards.front: When must you stop for a school or church bus?
cards.back: Meeting or following a school or church bus with red lights flashing and stop arm out, you must stop and stay stopped until the arm is withdrawn and the bus moves.

cards.front: What do flashing yellow lights on a school bus mean?
cards.back: Flashing yellow lights on a school bus mean it is about to stop to load or unload children, so slow down and get ready to stop.

cards.front: What is the penalty for passing a stopped school bus?
cards.back: Passing a stopped school bus is a Class A misdemeanor with a fine of two hundred fifty dollars to one thousand dollars.

cards.front: When need oncoming drivers not stop for a school bus?
cards.back: On a highway divided by a median or barrier, oncoming drivers need not stop for a school bus but must go carefully; a center turn lane is not a barrier, so traffic both ways must stop.

cards.front: Why must you never pass a stopped school bus on the right?
cards.back: Never pass a stopped school bus on the right, where children get on and off; stay stopped until it moves, its driver waves you on or its signals go off.

cards.front: Who must stop when a school bus loads at an intersection?
cards.back: When a school bus stops at an intersection to load or unload children, drivers coming from every direction must stop.

cards.front: Must you stop for a transit bus stopped for passengers?
cards.back: Unlike a school bus, a transit bus stopped for passengers does not require you to stop and may be passed, but watch for riders crossing.

decks.domain: Rules of the road: lights, speed, following, required stops and right-of-way

cards.front: Where do more crashes happen than anywhere else?
cards.back: More crashes happen at intersections than anywhere else, and the manual says intersections are involved in thirty-three percent of all crashes and twenty-one percent of fatal crashes.

cards.front: What is the left-right-left rule?
cards.back: Use the left-right-left rule at intersections: look left, then right, then left again just before moving, and look twice for motorcycles, bicycles and pedestrians.

cards.front: How should you approach an intersection?
cards.back: Slow before an intersection, be at your slowest just before entering, get into the correct lane beforehand, and never pass another vehicle inside an intersection.

cards.front: Is blocking an intersection after the light changes legal?
cards.back: Blocking an intersection after the light changes is always illegal, whether or not a sign says so.

cards.front: Does the law ever give anyone the right-of-way?
cards.back: The law never gives anyone the right-of-way; it only says who must yield, and you must still do everything possible to avoid a crash.

cards.front: What must you do for a pedestrian in a crosswalk in a flashing school zone?
cards.back: In a marked school zone with warning flashers on, you must stop for a pedestrian crossing in any crosswalk and stay stopped until they are across.

cards.front: How should you treat a pedestrian with a white cane or guide dog?
cards.back: For a pedestrian with a white or red-tipped cane or a guide dog, or a deaf walker whose dog wears a blaze orange leash, stop at least ten feet away and do not honk.

cards.front: When must you yield to pedestrians at corners and sidewalks?
cards.back: Yield to pedestrians crossing with the light when you turn a corner and when you cross a sidewalk from a driveway, alley or lot; driving on a sidewalk is illegal except to cross it.

cards.front: Where should you drive with extreme caution for children?
cards.back: Drive with extreme caution where children may be playing, and slow down near schools, playgrounds and residential areas.

cards.front: Whom must you yield to when turning left or leaving a driveway?
cards.back: When turning left, yield to oncoming traffic going straight or turning right, and when entering from a driveway or alley, yield to all traffic on the main road.

cards.front: Name other places where you must yield.
cards.back: Yield to traffic already in a roundabout, to moving traffic when leaving a parked position, to highway traffic when merging, and to an emergency vehicle backing into a fire station.

cards.front: Who goes first at an all-way stop?
cards.back: At an all-way stop the first vehicle to arrive goes first, and if two arrive together, yield to the vehicle on your right; at an uncontrolled crossing, also yield to the vehicle on your right.

cards.front: Whom must you yield to even on a green light?
cards.back: Yield to any vehicle already in the intersection even on your green, and on the dead-end road of a T intersection yield to traffic both ways on the main road.

decks.domain: Rules of the road: lights, speed, following, required stops and right-of-way

cards.front: What must you do for an emergency vehicle using a siren or flashing lights?
cards.back: Pull to the right edge and stop for any emergency vehicle using a siren, air horn or red or blue flashing light, and stay stopped until it passes or an officer waves you on.

cards.front: May private vehicles show blue flashing lights?
cards.back: Private vehicles may not carry or show blue, or blue and red, flashing emergency lights unless authorized.

cards.front: What rules apply around fire trucks answering an alarm?
cards.back: Never follow a fire truck answering an alarm, never drive within the block where it has stopped, and never run over a fire hose without permission from the officer in charge.

cards.front: What should you do for an emergency vehicle when you are in an intersection?
cards.back: For an emergency vehicle, clear the intersection before pulling over, avoid blocking a side road, and at a red light stay put even if it turns green before the vehicle passes.

cards.front: What should you do when a police car signals you to stop?
cards.back: When a police car signals you with flashing blue or blue and red lights or a siren, pull over close to the right edge, clear of any intersection, and stop.

cards.front: How should you behave during a traffic stop?
cards.back: During a traffic stop keep your hands on the wheel, keep passengers' hands visible, tell the officer if you hold a handgun permit and are armed, stay inside, and switch on the interior light after dark.

cards.front: What may you do if an unmarked car signals you to stop?
cards.back: Do not argue with an officer at the scene, since violations are decided in court, and if an unmarked car signals you, you may drive slowly to a nearby populated spot before stopping.
cards.memory_hook: Drive slowly to a public place

cards.front: When must you yield to a metro transit bus?
cards.back: Yield to a metro transit bus that has signaled and is pulling back into traffic from a bus stop.

cards.front: What does the Move Over Law require?
cards.back: Under the Move Over Law, on a road with two or more lanes your way, move out of the lane next to a stopped emergency, utility, road maintenance or tow vehicle with flashing lights, or slow to a safe speed.

cards.front: When does the Move Over requirement apply?
cards.back: The Move Over requirement applies only on roads with two or more lanes in your direction when the stopped vehicle is on your side of the road.

cards.front: What are the most common turning faults?
cards.back: The most common turning faults are not signaling, signaling too briefly, not searching for hazards, turning from the wrong lane and turning improperly.

cards.front: Which lanes should you turn from and into?
cards.back: Turn from the lane closest to your direction of turn into the closest legal lane, and remember that signaling never gives you the right-of-way.

cards.front: When do hand signals help, and when are they hard to see?
cards.back: Hand signals help in bright sun or heavy traffic but are hard to see at night, and you should pull your arm in to steer during the turn.

cards.front: What should you do before stopping and after turning?
cards.back: Tap the brakes a few times to flash your brake lights before stopping, and cancel your turn signal afterward so it does not mislead others.

recap_hooks.text: Headlights go on from thirty minutes after sunset to thirty minutes before sunrise, and dim within five hundred feet of another vehicle.
Never drive on parking lights alone when visibility is limited.
Your speed must always fit conditions and let you stop within the distance you can see.
Most rural interstates are posted at seventy miles per hour.
Speeding in a school zone is treated as reckless driving and adds six points.
Stay at least two seconds behind the car ahead, and four seconds in harder conditions.
With anti-lock brakes, press firmly and never pump.
A stop means all motion ends, and a rolling stop can earn a ticket.
When a train approaches, stop fifteen to fifty feet from the tracks.
Red lights and a stop arm on a school bus mean stop until the arm is withdrawn and the bus moves.
No one has the right-of-way; the law only says who must yield.
At an all-way stop the first to arrive goes first, and ties yield to the right.
Pull to the right and stop for emergency vehicles, and move over for stopped ones with flashing lights.
